paragraphs: 4KAgent approaches image enlargement as a sequence of decisions about restoration. It is designed to take images with varied resolutions and degradations to 4K, with further enlargement possible through repeated application. Its scope includes severely distorted, low-resolution inputs, making restoration planning an important part of the task.

The system combines three components. Profiling adapts the pipeline to the intended use. A perception agent combines vision-language models with image-quality assessment experts to inspect the input and propose a restoration plan. A restoration agent then executes and reassesses that plan, using a quality-guided mixture of experts to choose outputs at successive steps. A separate face-restoration pipeline improves facial details in portraits and selfies.

The authors evaluate 11 task categories across 26 benchmarks, spanning natural photographs, generated images, satellite imagery, microscopy, and medical images. They report leading results across a broad range of domains on both perceptual quality and fidelity measures. The contribution is a coordinated restoration system whose decisions adapt to the image and application.
neurips-2025-4kagent-agentic-any-image-t.tldr: 4KAgent coordinates image assessment, restoration planning, and specialist models to upscale diverse degraded images to 4K.

paragraphs: Machine learning and neuroscience can describe inference through equivalent objectives: maximizing an evidence lower bound corresponds to minimizing variational free energy. That agreement identifies what an inference system should optimize, but leaves open how a neural system could carry out the computation. This paper develops a framework that connects the objective to explicit neural dynamics.

The framework, FOND, combines natural-gradient optimization, online belief updates, and iterative refinement. From these principles, the authors derive iP-VAE, a recurrent spiking variational autoencoder. It updates its inferences through membrane-potential dynamics instead of relying on an amortized encoder to produce them directly. The theoretical analysis yields normalization through competition between neurons and integer spike-count representations suited to efficient hardware.

Experiments report improvements over standard VAEs and Gaussian predictive-coding models in reconstruction, sparsity, and biological plausibility. The model also handles complex color images and exceeds hybrid iterative-amortized VAEs on out-of-distribution inputs. These findings support deriving useful architectures from explicit inference principles while retaining features motivated by neural computation.
neurips-2025-brain-like-variational-infe.tldr: FOND derives iterative neural inference dynamics that produce a spiking VAE with strong reconstruction and generalization results.

paragraphs: Tree metrics describe distances as shortest paths through a tree, making them useful for representing hierarchical and combinatorial relationships. Real datasets can have distance structures that do not fit a tree exactly. The challenge is to find a tree-based representation that changes those distances as little as possible.

DeltaZero addresses this problem through differentiable optimization. Its central ingredient is a smooth substitute for Gromov hyperbolicity, a quantity that measures departure from tree-like distances. Smoothing this quantity makes it usable with gradient-based optimization while keeping the computation tractable. This supplies a direct optimization route for moving between an arbitrary metric and a tree metric.

The authors derive their procedure from a problem with improved worst-case guarantees relative to existing bounds and provide a statistical justification. On synthetic and real-world datasets, they report consistently leading distortion results. Here, distortion captures how much the resulting representation alters the original distances, so the reported improvements indicate better preservation of the relationships encoded by those distances.
neurips-2025-bridging-arbitrary-and-tree.tldr: DeltaZero uses a differentiable measure of tree-likeness to optimize tree metrics with strong guarantees and low empirical distortion.

paragraphs: Predicting what a scene will look like next can help systems understand changing environments. Producing every future pixel is computationally demanding, and it can direct effort toward details that do little to help scene understanding. DINO-Foresight instead predicts how the semantic features extracted by pretrained vision foundation models will evolve over time.

The framework trains a masked feature transformer using self-supervision. Its prediction target is the evolving feature representation, which serves as a latent space for future scenes. Existing task-specific heads can then operate on the predicted features to perform different kinds of future-frame analysis. This makes the forecasted representation useful through multiple attached heads.

The key design choice is to place forecasting between a pretrained visual representation and downstream scene-understanding components. This connects future prediction to features already useful for interpreting images. The authors report strong performance, robustness, and scalability in extensive experiments, supporting feature-space forecasting as a promising approach for applications such as autonomous driving and robotics.
neurips-2025-dino-foresight-looking-into.tldr: DINO-Foresight predicts future visual features that existing task heads can use for scene understanding.

paragraphs: Video outpainting extends a video beyond its original visible region. Keeping textures plausible is only part of the problem: objects and cameras move, and generated content must remain consistent across frames. This paper attributes common flickering and temporal inconsistencies to insufficient modeling of individual objects and their motion.

The proposed framework tracks objects together with their shadows. These pairs provide information for predicting where an instance occupies space even when it is temporarily invisible. The predictions then guide instance-aware optical-flow completion, which estimates the missing motion information. Together, the predicted locations and movements guide the outpainting process across space and time.

A video-aware discriminator further encourages agreement between moving shadows and the generated scene content. The approach matters because a shadow can contribute evidence about an object beyond the currently visible object itself. Experiments on established benchmarks report improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods, supporting the use of explicit shadow-object relationships to improve spatial and temporal consistency in dynamic video extensions.
neurips-2025-dynamic-shadow-unveils-invi.tldr: Tracking objects with their shadows helps video outpainting preserve the locations and motion of temporarily invisible instances.

paragraphs: This paper studies policy learning for agents that must coordinate online. Its focus is on how objective-function structure affects the quality guarantees available to a learning algorithm. The authors address both submodular objectives and weaker forms of submodularity, extending the range of coordination problems covered by their methods.

The first algorithm, MA-SPL, achieves the optimal 1 − c/e approximation guarantee for the studied submodular setting, where c is the objective's curvature. It also handles two weakly submodular settings characterized by additional ratios. The second algorithm, MA-MPL, removes dependence on those unknown parameters while retaining the same approximation ratio as MA-SPL.

Both algorithms use a policy-based continuous extension, which turns a discrete set-function problem into a continuous formulation. Its central advantage is a lossless rounding scheme for any set function, enabling the treatment of weakly submodular objectives. This general rounding property supports the algorithms, while their approximation claims remain tied to the stated objective classes. Simulations provide empirical evidence of their effectiveness.
neurips-2025-effective-policy-learning-f.tldr: Two online coordination algorithms extend approximation guarantees to weakly submodular objectives, with one eliminating unknown-parameter requirements.

paragraphs: Physical knowledge can guide a model through the loss function used during training. This paper develops that approach for prediction and generation involving systems such as molecules and spins. The aim is to make the training signal reflect the physical quality of a configuration while remaining independent of the model architecture.

The derivation assumes that each observed sample is in thermal equilibrium with respect to an approximate energy landscape. Using reverse KL divergence with a Boltzmann distribution around the data, the authors obtain a loss expressed as an energy difference between observations and predictions. They also interpret conventional mean squared error in energy terms, while arguing that its associated energy lacks physical meaning.

The proposed losses yield gradients better aligned with physically valid configurations and inherently respect physical symmetries. They are described as computationally efficient and applicable across architectures. Experiments on molecular generation and spin ground-state prediction show significant improvements over baselines, supporting physically informed training objectives under the formulation's stated equilibrium assumption.
neurips-2025-energy-loss-functions-for-p.tldr: Energy-based training losses incorporate physical knowledge directly into prediction and generation under an approximate thermal-equilibrium assumption.

paragraphs: Models of dynamical systems can struggle when training examples come from different environments. Methods designed to handle these differences often need labels identifying the environment behind each example. Such labels may be unavailable because of collection difficulties, privacy concerns, or changing conditions, limiting the usefulness of those generalization methods.

DynaInfer infers environment assignments from the data. Within each training round, it examines prediction errors from neural networks whose parameters are held fixed for that round. These error patterns provide the information used to infer environment specifications. The method therefore makes environment identification part of the learning procedure rather than requiring complete environment labels beforehand.

The authors prove that their algorithm solves the relevant alternating optimization problem in the unlabeled setting. Experiments across diverse dynamical systems report better results than existing assignment techniques and rapid convergence to true environment labels. They also report superior performance when environment labels are available, suggesting that the proposed inference procedure can remain useful even in that setting.
neurips-2025-environment-inference-for-l.tldr: DynaInfer uses prediction-error patterns to infer environments and improve dynamical-system learning without supplied environment labels.

paragraphs: Where a person looks provides clues about their attention, immediate intentions, and possible next actions. Gaze-VLM uses this information to train vision-language models for first-person understanding. The paper targets two tasks: describing the current activity and predicting fine-grained future events from an egocentric perspective.

The method introduces an attention regularizer that encourages the model's focus to align with human gaze during training. Gaze therefore shapes how the model learns to attend to visual information, without being required as an input at inference time. The mechanism is modular and can be used with multiple vision-language architectures that employ attention.

Compared with corresponding models trained without gaze regularization, the authors report semantic prediction-score improvements of up to 11% for future events and around 7% for current activities. These results support human gaze as a useful training signal for more accurate and robust first-person understanding. The work also motivates applications in assistive robotics and human-machine collaboration, where interpreting ongoing activity and anticipating what happens next can matter.
neurips-2025-gaze-vlm-bridging-gaze-and-.tldr: Gaze-VLM uses human gaze during training to improve first-person activity understanding and future-event prediction.

paragraphs: Generating detailed images and videos requires substantial computation. Progressive generation addresses this by building outputs from coarse structure toward finer detail. Explicit multistage systems can make that strategy cumbersome, however, because they may require specialized diffusion formulations, stage transitions, samplers, or cascades of separate models.

Decomposable Flow Matching applies flow matching independently at each level of a user-chosen multiscale representation, such as a Laplacian pyramid. The framework retains a single model and requires only small changes to existing training pipelines. Its contribution is a simpler way to organize progressive visual generation while preserving the advantages of multiple scales.

Experiments show improved image and video quality relative to prior multistage frameworks. On ImageNet-1k at 512-pixel resolution, the authors report FDD improvements of 35.2% over the base architecture and 26.4% over the strongest baseline using the same training compute. Fine-tuning experiments with large models such as FLUX also show faster convergence to the training distribution, indicating benefits beyond the initial generation experiments.
neurips-2025-improving-progressive-gener.tldr: Decomposable Flow Matching improves progressive image and video generation by applying flow matching across scales within a single model.

paragraphs: Treatment-effect estimation often relies on machine-learning estimates of supporting quantities, such as outcome regressions and treatment propensities. Structure-agnostic analysis studies what can be achieved when those estimates are treated as black boxes. This paper shows that, in a partially linear outcome model, the distribution of treatment noise changes the statistical limits.

For Gaussian treatment noise, the authors prove that double machine learning achieves the minimax-optimal rate. For independent non-Gaussian treatment noise, they show that it is suboptimal in the studied setting. They construct alternative ACE procedures that offer higher-order protection against errors in the supporting estimates, using structure-agnostic estimators of cumulants.

The robustness guarantee is conditional: ACE achieves r-th order insensitivity to nuisance errors whenever the treatment's (r+1)-st cumulant is nonzero. The paper also supplies minimax guarantees for binary treatments. Synthetic demand-estimation experiments demonstrate practical benefits from the higher-order estimators. Together, these results show why the treatment-noise distribution matters when choosing an estimator, even when nuisance models remain black boxes.
neurips-2025-its-hard-to-be-normal-the-i.tldr: Treatment-noise distributions determine whether double machine learning is rate-optimal or can be improved by higher-order robust estimators.

paragraphs: Generating a relational database requires preserving relationships across tables as well as realistic values within each table. Existing approaches often generate tables sequentially using adaptations of single-table models. The paper argues that this ordering limits parallelism and downstream flexibility, while conditional-independence assumptions can compound errors across the database.

The Graph-Conditional Relational Diffusion Model represents the database as a graph and models all tables jointly without imposing a table order. A graph neural network jointly denoises row attributes, allowing the generation process to capture dependencies across connected tables. This puts inter-table relationships inside the generative model itself.

Experiments on six real-world relational databases show substantial improvements over autoregressive baselines in capturing correlations that span multiple inter-table links. The model also achieves leading performance on single-table fidelity measures. These findings indicate that joint modeling can improve cross-table consistency while maintaining realistic individual tables, a useful combination for applications such as dataset augmentation and research on synthetic data release.
neurips-2025-joint-relational-database-g.tldr: GRDM jointly generates relational tables through graph-conditioned diffusion, improving both cross-table correlations and individual-table fidelity.

paragraphs: Large scenes represented through 3D Gaussian Splatting can demand substantial rendering time and GPU memory. LODGE addresses both costs with a hierarchy of detail levels. The system selects subsets of Gaussians according to camera distance, aiming to preserve useful visual detail while reducing the amount of scene information processed.

Each level is constructed using depth-aware three-dimensional smoothing, followed by importance-based pruning and fine-tuning. The smoothing and pruning reduce the representation, while fine-tuning helps maintain visual fidelity. The scene is also divided into spatial chunks so that rendering loads only relevant Gaussians. Opacity blending is used to prevent visible artifacts where chunks meet.

These mechanisms address complementary resource demands: detail selection reduces rendering work, and selective loading reduces memory overhead. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on outdoor Hierarchical 3DGS and indoor Zip-NeRF datasets, combining high-quality images with lower latency and memory requirements. The results support real-time rendering of large scenes on devices whose available memory would otherwise constrain the representation.
neurips-2025-lodge-level-of-detail-large.tldr: LODGE combines distance-dependent Gaussian detail with selective scene loading to reduce rendering latency and memory use.

paragraphs: Cooperative agents learning from demonstrations may receive a mixture of expert and suboptimal behavior without quality labels. Treating all demonstrations equally can obscure which behavior is worth imitating. This paper develops a two-stage approach that jointly addresses the identification of expert-quality trajectories and the learning of coordinated policies from the resulting labels.

The first stage combines large language models with preference-based reinforcement learning in a progressive labeling pipeline. The second stage uses MisoDICE, a multi-agent imitation algorithm built to handle the large joint state-action spaces that arise when several agents act together. It extends the single-agent DICE framework through a new value-decomposition and mixing architecture.

The formulation yields a convex policy-optimization objective and ensures consistency between global and local policies. That connection matters because the agents' individual policies must agree with the collective behavior being learned. Evaluations on standard multi-agent reinforcement-learning benchmarks report superior performance, particularly when expert demonstrations are scarce, supporting the combined labeling and imitation approach for mixed-quality offline data.
neurips-2025-misodice-multi-agent-imitat.tldr: MisoDICE combines trajectory-quality labeling with coordinated imitation learning to use mixed-quality demonstrations effectively.

paragraphs: Virtual try-on can leave traces of the original clothing or produce implausibly arranged body parts. This paper distinguishes these as inherent and acquired occlusions, respectively. Separating the two failure types lets the authors develop targeted operations within a mask-free framework for generating more convincing try-on images.

The first operation, background pre-replacement, helps prevent confusion between the target garment, the person's body, and the image background. It addresses lingering clothing artifacts. The second, covering-and-eliminating, strengthens the model's understanding of human semantic structure, helping it generate more realistic body parts and reducing structural disruptions.

The operations can be incorporated into different generative architectures, including GANs and diffusion models, and the method is applicable to in-the-wild settings. Experiments across three virtual try-on datasets show improvements in both qualitative and quantitative comparisons with recent methods. The contribution is a pair of adaptable interventions linked to distinct failure causes, allowing the same overall approach to address clothing remnants and malformed human structure.
neurips-2025-mitigating-occlusions-in-vi.tldr: A mask-free virtual try-on framework uses two targeted operations to reduce clothing remnants and implausible body structures.

paragraphs: Offline cooperative reinforcement learning requires agents to learn coordinated behavior from existing data. The challenge grows when many agents must cooperate over long sequences of actions. Oryx is designed to address both the number of interacting agents and the need for coherent decisions across multiple time steps.

The algorithm adapts the retention-based Sable architecture and combines it with a sequential version of implicit constraint Q-learning. Together, these components produce an offline autoregressive policy-update scheme. This sequence-oriented design supports complex coordination while maintaining temporal coherence along long trajectories, connecting how policies are updated with the structure of the behavior they must learn.

The evaluation spans SMAC, RWARE, and Multi-Agent MuJoCo, covering discrete and continuous control at different scales and difficulty levels. Oryx achieves state-of-the-art performance on more than 80% of 65 tested datasets. The authors also introduce datasets that further stress many-agent coordination and report strong scaling there, providing evidence for the method across demanding offline cooperative settings.
neurips-2025-oryx-a-scalable-sequence-mo.tldr: Oryx combines sequence modeling with offline policy learning to coordinate many agents over long trajectories.

paragraphs: PANTHER applies generative pretraining to sequences of user actions. Each action carries several attributes, such as time, context, and transaction type, creating sparse and irregular sequences with many possible values. The framework learns transferable representations from unlabeled behavioral data and adapts them for downstream prediction tasks.

Structured tokenization compresses transaction attributes into an interpretable vocabulary. A sequence-pattern module captures recurring transaction motifs, while a unified user embedding combines static demographics with changing transaction histories. The resulting framework supports personalized predictions and transfer of population-level knowledge. Caching pretrained embeddings offline enables millisecond-level inference for its operational use.

Deployed at WeChat Pay, PANTHER reports a 25.6% improvement in next-transaction HitRate@1 and a 38.6% relative improvement in fraud-detection recall over baselines. Evaluations on CCT, MBD, MovieLens-1M, and Yelp show gains of up to 21% in HitRate@1 over transformer baselines. These results support behavioral pretraining as a practical way to combine broad representation learning with task-specific predictions and fast serving.
neurips-2025-panther-generative-pretrain.tldr: PANTHER pretrains on user-action sequences to improve behavioral predictions while supporting millisecond-level inference.

paragraphs: Estimating large partial-correlation networks creates a demanding optimization problem. The paper builds on an existing l1-regularized pseudolikelihood framework that has statistical guarantees and scalability advantages over likelihood-based approaches. Its available implementations, however, use first-order information and can need thousands of iterations to obtain reliable estimates.

The authors develop semismooth Newton methods that use second-order information despite the objective's nonsmoothness. They establish local and global convergence properties, including a locally quadratic convergence rate. In practice, the methods require only a few tens of iterations. Each iteration involves small linear systems or smaller linear complementarity problems, helping keep the individual computational steps manageable.

Tests on simulated data and real genomic datasets show improved convergence behavior and computational efficiency. The smaller iteration subproblems also make the approach suitable for less powerful computing environments. The contribution strengthens the computational side of an existing estimation framework, making massive network analysis more practical for applications such as multi-omics research.
neurips-2025-partial-correlation-network.tldr: Semismooth Newton methods accelerate sparse partial-correlation network estimation with convergence guarantees and manageable iteration costs.

paragraphs: An agent both responds to past observations and acts to influence future observations. Empowerment captures the latter capacity. This paper develops a corresponding measure for the former: plasticity, understood as how and to what extent observations can influence an agent. The goal is to place both directions of influence within one mathematical framework.

Starting from requirements for a suitable definition, the authors introduce generalized directed information. They show that this quantity strictly extends the existing notion of directed information while retaining its desirable properties. Plasticity and empowerment can then be expressed using the same measure, with the direction of influence reversed.

The main result establishes a tension between an agent's plasticity and empowerment. This suggests that agent design should consider responsiveness to observations alongside the capacity to shape future observations. The contribution is a formal account of their relationship, giving the two capacities a shared basis for analysis and making their interaction part of the study of agency.
neurips-2025-plasticity-as-the-mirror-of.tldr: A new information-theoretic measure links an agent's responsiveness to observations with its ability to influence them.

paragraphs: A model that accepts images may still carry out its reasoning entirely through text. RBench-V evaluates a different capability: using visual outputs as part of solving a problem. The benchmark focuses on questions where manipulating or producing images is essential to the reasoning process, making visual generation part of the task itself.

The authors hand-select 803 questions across mathematics, physics, counting, and games. Required operations include creating new images and adding auxiliary lines to support a solution. This design shifts attention from the modality of the input toward what the model must produce and use while working through the problem.

Evaluations include multiple open- and closed-source models. The best tested model, o3, achieves 25.8% accuracy, compared with a human score of 82.3%. That gap indicates substantial difficulty with the benchmark's visual-reasoning demands. The results motivate evaluating multimodal systems on their ability to reason through visual transformations, alongside their ability to interpret images and provide text answers.
neurips-2025-rbench-v-a-primary-assessme.tldr: RBench-V tests reasoning that requires visual outputs and finds a large performance gap between evaluated models and humans.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can perform time-series forecasting and fill in missing observations, but repeated sampling steps add inference cost. This paper develops an operator-learning approach for conditioned time-series diffusion that generates an output in a single step. Its design draws on frequency structure in both the data and the diffusion process.

The authors describe forward diffusion as imposing frequency-dependent smoothing on the data's probability density. That smoothing is related to accessible frequency components of the time series. This relationship suggests that frequency-space modules may learn the reversal more effectively. The proposed learning task uses frequency-aware building blocks and satisfies semigroup properties, incorporating structure from the time series into the learned operator.

Across multiple datasets, single-step generation achieves forecasting and imputation results comparable to, or better than, many multistep diffusion schemes while substantially reducing inference costs. The evidence supports the proposed frequency-aware design as an efficient sampling approach. The motivation remains appropriately conditional: frequency structure suggests a useful route to learning the reversal, while the experiments establish its observed benefits.
neurips-2025-single-step-operator-learni.tldr: Frequency-aware operator learning enables single-step time-series diffusion with competitive forecasting and imputation quality at lower inference cost.

paragraphs: Learning useful representations of movement trajectories across cities is difficult because road networks, spatial grids, and traffic rules differ. Combining multiple views of trajectory data can enrich a representation, but it introduces competing demands. Improving performance for one city, view, or task may worsen it for another, creating the paper's seesaw problem.

SMARTraj² addresses these issues through feature disentanglement and personalized gating. The disentanglement module separates features shared across environments from features specific to an environment. The gating mechanism dynamically stabilizes the contributions of different views and tasks. Together, these components support shared learning while accommodating differences between urban settings.

Benchmark experiments report stronger cross-city generalization and improvements over state-of-the-art methods, alongside robust performance across multiple downstream tasks. The findings support treating transfer and training balance as connected problems: a representation needs to capture common patterns while controlling how competing sources of information contribute. This is relevant to deploying trajectory models across heterogeneous cities for transportation, planning, and environmental applications.
neurips-2025-smartraj-2-a-stable-multi-c.tldr: SMARTraj² separates shared and city-specific features while balancing data views and tasks to improve cross-city trajectory learning.

paragraphs: Scene text recognition produces a sequence of characters, so an attack that changes only a few characters may leave much of the original information intact. A dictionary or language model can potentially repair those errors. This paper investigates attacks intended to disrupt each character, addressing the recoverability of partially corrupted recognition outputs.

The proposed Multi-Population Coevolution Search divides a global optimization objective into smaller objectives. This distributed approach addresses the tendency of previous attacks to concentrate changes in particular image pixels. Distributing the optimization creates an additional difficulty, described as joint perturbation shift. The authors introduce a coevolution energy function to address this interaction among the perturbations.

Experiments on recent scene-text recognizers report superior attack performance. The methodological contribution is to combine character-level attack objectives with coordination across their joint image modifications. The results support more extensive disruption of recognized text; the paper's stated aim of moving toward irreversible attacks should be read alongside that empirical claim, rather than as a universal guarantee against recovery.
neurips-2025-towards-irreversible-attack.tldr: MPCS coordinates distributed character-level objectives to produce more disruptive attacks on scene text recognition.

paragraphs: This paper studies predicting first-person video from past video and human actions. The actions are represented through relative three-dimensional body pose, giving the model an explicit description of bodily movement. The task connects video prediction with the question of how physical actions shape what a person subsequently sees.

The model conditions on pose trajectories organized by the body's joint hierarchy. This supplies structured movement information across the whole body. The authors train an autoregressive conditional diffusion transformer on Nymeria, which contains real-world egocentric video paired with body-pose capture. The training setup links observed visual sequences with the physical movements accompanying them.

The paper also introduces a hierarchical evaluation protocol whose tasks become progressively more challenging. That protocol is designed to analyze embodied prediction and control capabilities across different demands. The work is presented as an initial attempt at modeling complex real-world environments and embodied behavior through human-viewpoint video prediction. Its central contribution is the combination of structured whole-body conditioning and an evaluation framework for this prediction setting.
neurips-2025-whole-body-conditioned-egoc.tldr: A conditional video model uses structured whole-body pose trajectories to predict first-person visual consequences of human actions.

paragraphs: Post-training adapts language models to preferences and tasks, but it can also make their confidence less reliable. A post-trained model may assign high confidence to incorrect answers as well as correct ones. DACA addresses the difficulty of correcting this behavior when labeled examples for each downstream task are scarce.

The method uses the pretrained model as an unsupervised reference for post-hoc confidence calibration. Directly aligning the two models' confidence can go wrong when their predictions disagree. The paper's theoretical analysis shows that pretrained-model confidence underestimates post-trained-model accuracy on disagreement examples, pushing the temperature parameter too high and making predictions underconfident. DACA calibrates using only examples on which the models agree.

Selecting agreement examples separates calibration from this disagreement effect and avoids the associated overly large temperature. Experiments on open-source and API-based models report improvements in average expected calibration error of up to 15.08% on common benchmarks. The findings support selective use of pretrained confidence as a way to improve post-trained confidence estimates without task-specific labeled calibration data.
neurips-2025-your-pre-trained-llm-is-sec.tldr: DACA calibrates post-trained language models without labels by aligning confidence only where pretrained and post-trained predictions agree.
